name: Adam Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Greenway Growers, a big vegetable farm that grows lettuce, broccoli and leeks for two supermarket chains. This time of year it's leeks, so I'm out at seven on the harvest rig, a slow trailer that crawls along the rows while a crew pulls, trims and boxes. Afternoons I'm usually in the packhouse, stacking pallets and checking labels, because if the supermarket's label is wrong the whole load gets sent back.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Three years. Before that I drove the number 14 bus for twenty-five years, until my eyes failed the medical for night driving. My son set me up with an app to search jobs, and Greenway came up. I'm still the new boy, they let me drive the rig tractor but only at walking pace, which suits me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the crew. Half of them come over each season from abroad, and I've learned to say good morning in four languages. What wears me out is the supermarket. They change the box size or the spec, the rules for how big a leek must be, with two days' notice, and we all run around like mad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, I use it already, every day. I use an AI app on my phone to translate for the crew, and to check photos of leaves when something looks off. I'd tell my mates it's a good tool and stop being scared of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job gets a bit easier and nothing else changes. That's fine by me. The real problem at Greenway isn't computers, it's the price the supermarket pays for a head of broccoli.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the packhouse manager, Sunita, if I can set up the translation thing on the shared tablet for the whole crew, not just me. I'd keep saving, we've got about four months put by. And I'd keep pushing to get on the forklift rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit pleased with myself, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about a time the translation app actually helped.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring a lad called Petya cut his hand badly on a trimming knife and he was in shock, talking fast in Bulgarian. I held the phone up and it told me he was asking if he'd lose his job. I said no, and I watched his shoulders drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the real problem is the supermarket. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They set the price, the size, the date, everything. Last year they knocked two pence off a lettuce in the middle of the season, and Greenway cut the crew's overtime to make up for it. No AI did that, a buyer in an office did.

S0.say: I'd say I already use it every day to translate for the crew and to check leaf photos. I'd tell my mates it's a good tool and to stop being scared.
S0.think: I think my job just gets a bit easier and nothing else changes. The real problem at Greenway is the price the supermarket pays, not computers.
S0.do: Asks the packhouse manager to set up translation on the shared tablet for the whole crew. Keeps saving about four months' worth and pushes to get on the forklift rota.
S0.feel: Calm, and a little pleased with himself.
S0.quote: I held the phone up and it told me he was asking if he'd lose his job. I said no, and I watched his shoulders drop.
S0.fieldNote: Adam is the rare 58-year-old beginner who uses AI more than his bosses do. His instinct is to share the tool with the crew rather than keep the advantage. His anger points clearly at the supermarket buyers, not at technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. Second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms already hire fewer beginners from here, they hire them from abroad for the season. I'd say if tasks disappear, the crew should share the time saved, not lose the hours. I'd put that on the union page on Facebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it probably helps me a bit. If tasks disappear slowly, the ones that need a bit of tech go to whoever can use it, and that's me, oddly. But I feel bad saying that, because it's the seasonal lads who'd lose the hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Sunita if I could be the one who trains the crew on new kit as it comes. I'd do a free online course on food safety records, they're all going digital. And I'd talk to the union rep about getting the seasonal workers proper written terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little guilt mixed in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why guilt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've got a pension from the bus company and a wife who's a nurse. Petya's sending money home to two kids. If anyone should get the new jobs, it's probably not the old man with a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ruth say about you training the crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say, Adam, you can't even set the clock on the oven. And she'd be right, but that's different, the oven's got buttons from 1998. She'd be proud though, she'd tell her friends at the hospital.

S1.say: I'd say farms already hire beginners from abroad for the season, and the crew should share any time saved instead of losing hours. I'd post that on the union page.
S1.think: I think slow change probably helps me, because tech tasks go to whoever can use them. But I feel bad, because the seasonal workers would lose the hours.
S1.do: Asks to be the one who trains the crew on new kit and does a free online course on digital food safety records. Talks to the union rep about written terms for seasonal workers.
S1.feel: Calm, with some guilt about doing better than younger seasonal workers.
S1.quote: If anyone should get the new jobs, it's probably not the old man with a cushion.
S1.fieldNote: His adaptability gives him an edge here and he knows it, which makes him uncomfortable. He keeps measuring his luck against Petya's. He's honest that his partner's nursing job and his bus pension shape how safe he feels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the third. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when nobody's in charge. The politicians should stop shouting and do something, a shorter week, help for people retraining, something. I'd say it loudly on the union page and at the dinner table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be thinking about my son Josh. He's a freelance graphic designer, he does logos and menus for cafés, and the AI already does a lot of that. He's thirty and he hasn't got much of a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Josh and look at what he can sell that the AI can't, like painting shop signs by hand or doing the big murals. I'd lend him a month's rent if he asked. And at Greenway I'd ask about the new jobs, whoever looks after the order system and the labels, because that's all screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me, for Josh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd ask about the label and order work. Isn't that office work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, yes, you've got me. It's the office end of a farm, so maybe it goes the same way. I suppose I'd want to be the person who checks the AI got the label right, because when it's wrong, it's the lorry that comes back, not the computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Josh on the phone, the day he lost a big client?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say come up for Sunday lunch and bring your laptop. Then I'd make him show me the AI that took his job, because I want to see it. Ruth would tell me that's not helpful, and she'd probably be right.

S2.say: I'd say this is what happens when nobody's in charge, and politicians should stop shouting and act. A shorter week or help with retraining, something.
S2.think: Privately I'd be thinking about my son Josh, a freelance graphic designer without much cushion. The AI already does a lot of his logo and menu work.
S2.do: Helps Josh find work AI can't do, like hand-painted signs and murals, and would lend him a month's rent. Asks Greenway about the order and label work and offers to be the one who checks the AI's labels.
S2.quote: When it's wrong, it's the lorry that comes back, not the computer.
S2.fieldNote: He accepted the contradiction cheerfully and turned it into a job idea on the spot, which is very him. His curiosity even extends to wanting to see the AI that took his son's clients. The worry is real but it's about Josh, not himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The fourth one is faster. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains should be taxed and shared, simple as that. If shares and houses boom while people lose jobs, then the people who own the shares should pay for the people who lost the jobs. I'd join the march, Ruth would come too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd also notice that my little bus pension is partly in shares, so I'd be doing well out of it, which is a strange feeling. And the supermarkets would be swimming in money while still knocking pence off our lettuces. That's the part that'd make me angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check what the pension's worth and leave it alone, no gambling. I'd give Ellie, my daughter, something toward her flat deposit if prices were climbing, before they climbed further. And I'd push at work for the crew's pay to go up, because the supermarkets could afford it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit ashamed of doing well out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd do well out of the boom but you'd march against it. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, but it's the honest answer. I'd rather pay more tax on my pension than watch Josh and his mates go under. I don't think wanting fairness means you have to be poor first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Physical jobs are mostly untouched here. Does that make you feel safe at Greenway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the moment, yes. Nobody's coming for the leek crew with a chatbot. But I've seen the camera hoe, the machine that weeds by looking at the plants, so I don't feel safe for long.

S3.say: I'd say the gains should be taxed and shared, with share owners paying for those who lost jobs. I'd join the march with Ruth.
S3.think: I'd notice my bus pension is partly in shares, so I'd be doing well, which feels strange. The supermarkets would be rich while still squeezing what they pay for lettuces.
S3.do: Checks his pension and leaves it alone, and helps his daughter Ellie with a flat deposit before prices climb further. Pushes for the crew's pay to rise.
S3.feel: Uneasy, and a bit ashamed of doing well from a boom he'd protest against.
S3.quote: I don't think wanting fairness means you have to be poor first.
S3.fieldNote: He was candid that he'd gain from the boom, and he didn't wriggle when I pointed at the gap. His anger keeps landing on the supermarkets. The camera hoe came up for the first time, and it clearly sits in the back of his mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. This is the last one. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots on farms are coming whether we like it or not, so the fight is over who owns them and who shares the money. I'd say the seasonal workers must get help, because they'll be hit first. And I'd say it at every meeting I can get to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd put my hand up to run the robot. Better me learning it at fifty-eight than the farm hiring a lad from the city to babysit it. But I know the crew of twenty becomes a crew of four, and I'd be one of the four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Sunita the first week and ask to go on the training for the robot harvesters, before anyone else. I'd learn the camera hoe properly, I already watch it on YouTube. And I'd push the union to get the seasonal lads a payout and help to find other work, because they won't be coming back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and excited at the same time, which is a horrible mix. I'd be sleeping fine and feeling bad about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Petya, if he wasn't coming back next season?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd message him in Bulgarian with the app, so it's in his words, not mine. I'd say I'm sorry and I'd mean it. And I'd ask if there's anything I can send, which is probably nothing, which is the worst part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the training goes to someone younger?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be on the rig until there isn't a rig, and then I'd look for something else. There are a few other growers nearby, and I can always drive a minibus for a school. I'm not proud, I've driven a bus full of drunk students at two in the morning.

S4.say: I'd say farm robots are coming, so the fight is over who owns them and who shares the money. Seasonal workers must get help because they'll be hit first.
S4.think: Off the record I'd put my hand up to run the robot rather than let the farm hire a lad from the city. But a crew of twenty becomes four, and I'd be one of the four.
S4.do: Asks in the first week to train on the robot harvesters and learns the camera hoe properly. Pushes the union for payouts and job help for seasonal workers.
S4.feel: Anxious and excited at once, sleeping fine and feeling guilty about it.
S4.quote: I'd put my hand up to run the robot. Better me learning it at fifty-eight than the farm hiring a lad from the city to babysit it.
S4.fieldNote: Adam is the most hopeful hands-on worker I've met in this group, but his hope comes with guilt. He'd fight for the people the robots replace while signing up to run them. His fallback plan, driving a minibus, shows he isn't relying on the robot job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, because of the crew more than me. What would help is a proper fund, paid by the farms and the supermarkets, that gives seasonal workers a payout and training when the machines arrive. And training for older workers like me that isn't just a link to a website.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the supermarkets, and they're behind all of it. Whatever happens with AI, a buyer in an office decides what a leek is worth. If you want to change something, start there.

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Any time. Tell your readers to buy the wonky leeks, they taste the same.

headlineQuote: I'd put my hand up to run the robot. Better me learning it at fifty-eight than the farm hiring a lad from the city to babysit it.
portrait: Adam is a 58-year-old former bus driver who now works on the harvest rig and in the packhouse at a large vegetable grower supplying supermarkets. He uses AI every day, mostly to translate for the seasonal crew, and he blames supermarket buyers far more than technology. As the scenarios speed up, he worries for his freelance designer son and for the seasonal workers, and admits he'd gain from a share boom. With farm robots, he'd volunteer to run them first, and feels guilty about it.
biggestWorry: The robot picture worries him most, because a crew of twenty becomes four and the seasonal workers would be hit first.
whatWouldHelp: A fund paid by farms and supermarkets to give seasonal workers a payout and training, and real hands-on training for older workers.
